newsitem.title: USA: U.S forecasters warn of possible El Nino this year.
newsitem.headline: U.S forecasters warn of possible El Nino this year.

text.p: Forecasters will know next month if unusually warm ocean temperatures have spawned an "El Nino" weather pattern that could produce flooding and droughts in parts of the western hemisphere and as far away as Africa, U.S. officials said on Thursday.

"If these temperatures persist for another month or two, it would be accurate to say that we're already in an El Nino," said Vern Kousky, a weather expert with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's climate prediction centre.
The agency will issue an updated forecast on June 10 to announce whether an El Nino will threaten North and South America, he said.

The combination of warm Pacific Ocean temperatures and a shift in the atmospheric jet stream means that certain areas with typically dry conditions will instead get heavy rain and potential flooding, while other regions can be drought-stricken.
An El Nino occurs every two to seven years, reversing normal weather patterns throughout areas of Canada, the United States, Mexico, South America and as far away as Africa.

The last major El Nino occurred in late 1991 through mid-1992, with a smaller and less destructive El Nino recorded in 1994-95, Kousky said. The weather system can last as long as 18 months, depending on how rapidly the ocean temperatures cool down and return to normal.
"We're ripe for another one," Kousky said.
The change in weather from a major El Nino can have a devastating impact on agriculture, fishing, tourism and local economies.

The strongest El Nino this century was recorded in 1982-83, and caused an estimated $8.1 billion in damage from flooding, drought and unusual hurricane activity, according to government estimates. California alone reported some $1.3 billion in damage from a series of heavy storms and flooding.
"We have better forecasting techniques now that mean farmers can prepare for these weather changes by planting different crops, storing up water supplies or grain reserves in advance," Kousky said.
U.S. weather forecasters collect data on ocean and atmospheric temperatures from a network of buoys in the Pacific that also monitor currents and winds.

The abnormal weather pattern was nicknamed "El Nino" after fishermen along the coasts of Peru and Ecuador noticed a warming in ocean temperatures around the Christmas holiday. The phrase is Spanish for "Christ Child."
